title: Titus

stories.title: 📜 Titus 1
summaryBullets: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, (1:1).
in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began. (1:2).
In His own time He has made His word evident in the proclamation entrusted to me by the command of God our Savior. (1:3).
To Titus, my true child in our common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior. (1:4).
The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you. (1:5).
An elder must be blameless, the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers and who are not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination. (1:6).
As God’s steward, an overseer must be above reproach — not self-willed, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not greedy for money. (1:7).
Instead, he must be hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. (1:8).
He must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it. (1:9).
For many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision, (1:10).
who must be silenced. For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not. (1:11).
As one of their own prophets has said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” (1:12).
This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith (1:13).
and will pay no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of men who have rejected the truth. (1:14).
To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled. (1:15).
They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him. They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed. (1:16).
crossRefs: Matthew 7:15–20: False teachers known by their fruits.
Romans 14:20: All things clean, but it is wrong to cause stumbling.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זָקֵן (zāqēn) / פָּקִיד (pāqîd, sense), Greek: πρεσβύτερος (presbýteros) / ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, NT), Aramaic: קשישא (qašīšā) / אפיסקופא (episqopā)
translationNotes.note: Elder highlights maturity and community standing; overseer (bishop) emphasizes stewardship and responsibility.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טָהוֹר / טָמֵא (ṭāhôr / ṭāmēʾ), Greek: καθαρός / μίαντος (katharós / míantos, NT), Aramaic: דכיא / מסאב (dakkīyā / msāʾb)
translationNotes.note: Biblical categories of clean versus unclean; here used morally and spiritually.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul charges Titus to appoint qualified elders and silence false teachers in Crete, contrasting purity of faith with corrupted unbelief.

stories.title: 🌿 Titus 2
summaryBullets: But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine. (2:1).
Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. (2:2).
Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good. (2:3).
In this way they can train the young women to love their husbands and children, (2:4).
to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited. (2:5).
In the same way, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. (2:6).
In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works. In your teaching show integrity, dignity, (2:7).
and wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us. (2:8).
Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, (2:9).
not stealing from them, but showing all good faith, so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior. (2:10).
For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. (2:11).
It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age, (2:12).
as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. (2:13).
He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds. (2:14).
Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you. (2:15).
crossRefs: Ephesians 5:25–27: Christ gave himself to sanctify the church.
Philippians 3:20: Awaiting the Savior from heaven.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד אֱלֹהִים נִגְלָה (ḥesed ʾĕlōhîm niglāh, sense), Greek: ἐπεφάνη ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ (epephánē hē cháris tou theoû, NT), Aramaic: אתגליאת טיבותא דאלהא (ʾetgalyāṯ ṭīḇūṯā d-ʾAlāhā)
translationNotes.note: Describes God’s saving grace revealed historically in Christ’s coming.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַתִּקְוָה הַבְּרוּכָה (hattiqwāh habbərūḵāh, sense), Greek: μακαρία ἐλπίς (makaría elpís, NT), Aramaic: סִבְרָא טָבָא (sibrā ṭāḇā)
translationNotes.note: Refers to the future hope of Christ’s glorious appearing.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul instructs Titus to teach different groups to live godly lives, grounded in the grace and redemption of Christ who is coming again.

stories.title: 🕊️ Titus 3
summaryBullets: Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, (3:1).
to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone. (3:2).
For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures — living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. (3:3).
But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, (3:4).
He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. (3:5).
This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, (3:6).
so that, having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life. (3:7).

This saying is trustworthy. And I want you to emphasize these things, so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds. These things are excellent and profitable for the people. (3:8).
But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless. (3:9).
Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition, (3:10).
knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned. (3:11).
As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there. (3:12).
Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need. (3:13).
And our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful. (3:14).
All who are with me send you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with all of you. (3:15).
crossRefs: Romans 13:1: Be subject to governing authorities.
John 3:5: Born of water and Spirit.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רַחֲצָה לְחִדּוּשׁ (raḥăṣāh leḥiddūš, sense), Greek: λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας (loutròn palingenesías, NT), Aramaic: סחיתא דאתחדשותא (saḥyṯā d-ʾiṯḥaddašūṯā)
translationNotes.note: Phrase for new birth through the Spirit’s work, depicted as cleansing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חִדּוּשׁ בָּרוּחַ (ḥiddūš bārūaḥ, sense), Greek: ἀνακαίνωσις πνεύματος (anakáinōsis pneúmatos, NT), Aramaic: חדתותא דרוחא (ḥaddāṯūṯā d-rūḥā)
translationNotes.note: Speaks of inner transformation by the Spirit making believers new.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִישׁ מַחֲלוֹקֶת (ʾîš maḥălōqeṯ, sense), Greek: αἱρετικὸς ἄνθρωπος (hairetikòs ánthrōpos, NT), Aramaic: גברא פלוגתא (gabrā pelūgṯā, sense)
translationNotes.note: Term for one who causes factions; Paul instructs rejection after repeated warnings.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul urges believers to live peaceably, remembering God’s saving mercy, while avoiding fruitless controversies and divisive people.

intro:
Titus was written by Paul the apostle (Titus 1:1), the third of the Pastoral Epistles (along with 1 Timothy and 2 Timothy), addressed to Paul's Gentile coworker Titus who was overseeing the churches on the island of Crete. The letter was composed around AD 63-65, after Paul's release from his first Roman imprisonment and during the same fourth missionary journey period in which Paul wrote 1 Timothy; Paul mentions in Titus 3:12 that he is planning to spend the winter at Nicopolis in western Greece, suggesting the letter was written from Macedonia or another point on Paul's journey westward. Paul had himself visited Crete with Titus on this journey, planted or strengthened churches in the cities there, and left Titus behind with instructions to "put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you" (Titus 1:5). Titus was a Gentile believer (a Greek by birth; Galatians 2:3 specifies him as "uncircumcised") who had become one of Paul's most trusted coworkers. He had been with Paul as a test case at the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, where Paul had taken him as a Gentile believer who had not been required to be circumcised in order to be a Christian (Galatians 2:1-3 describes this visit). Titus had served as Paul's troubleshooter and courier during the Corinthian crisis (mentioned nine times in 2 Corinthians, including 2 Corinthians 7:6-7, 13-15 and 8:6, 16-23), carrying letters between Paul and the Corinthian church and helping to resolve the dispute. After this letter, Titus would later be sent to Dalmatia on the Adriatic coast (2 Timothy 4:10). According to ancient tradition, Titus became the first bishop of Crete and continued ministering on the island for the rest of his life; he died peacefully at age ninety-four around AD 96 at Gortyna (the Roman provincial capital of Crete) and was buried there. His skull is venerated today at the Cathedral of Saint Titus in Heraklion, Crete. Paul (originally Saul) was born in Tarsus of Cilicia around AD 5-10 to a Hebrew family of the tribe of Benjamin, educated in Jerusalem under Gamaliel the Pharisee before his conversion on the Damascus road and his apostolic ministry to the Gentiles; he was martyred by beheading in Rome under Nero around AD 66-67 (see the introduction to Romans for the full biographical sketch).

The historical setting is the island of Crete in the Roman province of Creta et Cyrenaica (Crete and Cyrenaica). Crete is the largest of the Greek islands and the fifth-largest island in the Mediterranean, lying about 160 miles south of mainland Greece and 200 miles north of the African coast. The island had a long and storied history as the seat of the Bronze Age Minoan civilization (c. 3000-1100 BC), the legendary home of King Minos and the labyrinth of the Minotaur, and a major maritime power in the second millennium BC. Crete had been a Roman province since 67 BC, when the Roman general Quintus Caecilius Metellus conquered the island (gaining the cognomen "Creticus" for his victory); under Augustus the province was joined with Cyrenaica on the North African coast to form the senatorial province of Creta et Cyrenaica, with its provincial capital at Gortyna in south-central Crete. The Cretans had a notorious reputation in the ancient world for dishonesty; Paul quotes a Cretan poet (Titus 1:12: "One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons'") which is a line from Epimenides of Knossos, a sixth- or seventh-century BC Cretan philosopher and prophet whose verse on Cretan duplicity had become proverbial across the Greek-speaking world (Cretans were also said to have lied about Zeus's tomb being on Crete; the Greek verb krētizein, "to Cretize," meant "to lie"). Despite or because of this difficult cultural soil, Paul left Titus to plant durable churches in the Cretan cities and to address the practical concerns of pastoral leadership in a notoriously rough culture.

Titus is the fifty-sixth book of the Christian Bible, the seventeenth book of the New Testament, and the twelfth of Paul's thirteen letters in canonical order. It is the third and final of the Pastoral Epistles. The letter has three chapters, making it the shortest of the three Pastoral Epistles. The earliest surviving manuscript of Titus is Papyrus 32 (P32, c. AD 200), a small fragment of Titus 1:11-15 and 2:3-8 housed at the John Rylands Library in Manchester; other early witnesses include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD). Several of Titus's passages have become foundational to Christian doctrine: Titus 1:5-9 lists the character qualifications for elders (overlapping with but distinct from 1 Timothy 3); Titus 2:11-14 is one of the most concentrated New Testament statements of the gospel of grace and an explicit affirmation of Christ's full deity (the Greek phrase translated "our great God and Savior Jesus Christ" in 2:13 grammatically applies both titles, "God" and "Savior," to Jesus Himself under the Granville Sharp rule, when two singular nouns are joined by kai and only the first carries the article): "For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession, who are zealous for good works"; and Titus 3:4-7 ("But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit").
